title: Spatial Proteomic Profiling Reveals Increased Levels of Cholesterol Synthesis Proteins in Psoriasis Vulgaris
projectDescription: Background and Aims: Chronic plaque psoriasis results from genetic and environmental factors that activate inflammatory pathways involving both innate and adaptive immunity. Although the histological features are well known, protein-level changes—especially with spatial resolution—are less understood. This study aimed to investigate layer-specific proteomic changes in psoriatic skin.  Methods: Skin biopsies from psoriasis patients (N=8) and healthy controls (N=8) were separated into four layers (stratum corneum, inner epidermis, dermis, subcutis) using laser-capture microdissection. Proteins were extracted and analyzed by mass spectrometry.  Results: We identified 7,236 proteins, with 1,649 differentially expressed in lesional vs. non-lesional inner epidermis. Upregulated proteins were linked to innate immunity, cholesterol synthesis and tissue structure. The stratum corneum in lesions showed more complex protein profiles than in controls. The dermis displayed increased proteins related to IL-17 signaling and neutrophil recruitment. No significant changes were found in the subcutis.  Conclusion: This dataset highlights the inner epidermis as a key site of proteomic alterations in psoriasis, driven by proteins related to immune activity, tissue structure and cholesterol synthesis. The layer-specific approach offers detailed spatial insights into disease-associated protein changes.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Cell-type resolved Deep Visual Proteomics was conducted as described previously (Mund and Coscia et al., Nature Biotechnology, 2022) using laser capture microdissection on formalin-fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) tissue. Sample Preparation: Laser capture microdissection (Leica LMD7) was performed on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) skin biopsies to isolate four distinct layers: stratum corneum, inner epidermis (excluding stratum corneum), dermis (including dermal papillae), and subcutis. Microdissected areas were manually annotated using Leica V8.2.3 software and collected into 384-well plates. A median of 462,844 µm² tissue per sample was obtained.  Protein Extraction and Digestion: Sample preparation followed the Deep Visual Proteomics (DVP) protocol using an Agilent Bravo liquid handling robot. Samples were processed semi-automatically for protein extraction and digested with trypsin overnight. Following digestion, samples were either vacuum dried and stored at –20°C or resuspended in 4 µL of buffer A* (3% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid).  Chromatography and Mass Spectrometry: Peptides were analyzed using an EASY-nLC 1200 system coupled to a timsTOF SCP mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics) with a CaptiveSpray ion source. Samples were loaded from 384-well plates and separated on a 50-cm C18 column (75 µm i.d., 1.9 µm ReproSil-Pur C18-AQ beads, Dr. Maisch) using a 70-minute gradient. Buffer B (80% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid) increased from 5% to 30% over 55 minutes, followed by a wash at 95% B. Buffer A was 0.1% formic acid in water; flow rate was 300 nL/min. Column temperature was maintained at 60°C using a custom oven. InstrumentAcquisitionSettings: Data acquisition was performed in both data-dependent (ddaPASEF) and data-independent (diaPASEF) modes. • ddaPASEF: 1 MS1 scan followed by 10 PASEF MS/MS scans; singly charged ions excluded using a polygon filter. • diaPASEF: 20 PASEF MS/MS scans; precursor isolation windows: 2 Th for m/z <700 and 3 Th for m/z >700. • TIMS settings: Ion accumulation and ramp time set to 100 ms; ion mobility range: 1/K₀ = 1.6 to 0.6 V·s/cm²; collision energy stepped from 59 eV to 20 eV with increasing mobility. • Scan range: m/z 100–1700.
dataProcessingProtocol: Library Generation and Search: DDA files from all skin layers were searched using MSFragger (v18.0) with IonQuant (v1.8.9) and Philosopher (v4.2.2). Cysteine carbamidomethylation was set as a fixed modification; methionine oxidation, N-terminal acetylation, and phosphorylation (S, T, Y) were allowed as variable modifications (up to three per peptide). Trypsin was used as the enzyme, allowing up to two missed cleavages. FDR was controlled at 1% for PSM, peptide, and protein levels. The search database was UniProt (2019, UP000005640_9606, 20,594 genes). The final spectral library contained 286,575 precursors and 11,944 protein groups.  Quantification and Analysis: DIA files were analyzed using DIA-NN (v1.8.1) in library-based mode. Match-between-runs (MBR) and retention time-based normalization were enabled. Parameters included: • Enzyme: trypsin, 1 missed cleavage • Variable modifications: N-terminal Met excision, oxidation, acetylation (max 2) • Peptide length: 7–30 amino acids • Precursor charge: 2–4 • Quantification: ‘robust LC (high precision)’ mode • Output: Four separate *.pg_matrix.tsv files, one per skin layer (outer epidermis, inner epidermis, dermis, subcutis)
